parsed_answer.content: Prior to Java 9, creating unmodifiable or constant collections required verbose, boilerplate-heavy code like Collections.unmodifiableList(Arrays.asList("a", "b")) or cumbersome anonymous inner class double-brace initialization. These legacy approaches had severe architectural flaws: they merely wrapped mutable backing collections (meaning changes to the underlying array still mutated the view), and they suffered from significant heap overhead due to object allocation, pointer indirections, and lack of compact memory layout. To solve this, Java 9 introduced factory methods directly on the interface level: List.of(), Map.of(), and Set.of(). These methods provide truly immutable collections with zero null tolerance, optimized memory footprints, structural uniqueness enforcement, and fail-fast iteration guarantees.

Under the hood, these factory methods do not return standard collection implementations like ArrayList, HashSet, or HashMap. Instead, they leverage hidden value-based and compact internal implementations (such as ImmutableCollections.ListN, List12, or specialized power-of-two capacity Map implementations). Because these collections are unmodifiable, they can optimize hash tables and array storage, eliminating the need for load factor overhead, chaining node allocations, or synchronization guards. Furthermore, attempting to insert a null value into any of these collections instantly throws a NullPointerException, aligning with modern API design principles that reject ambiguous null sentinel values.

rows: Read-only view; mutable if the backing collection changes
Deeply immutable; structurally frozen at creation
Permits nulls if the backing collection does
Low (compact array structures, zero extra wrapper overhead)
Set.of() and Map.of() throw IllegalArgumentException on duplicates

items: Iteration order in Map.of() and Set.of() is intentionally randomized per JVM execution (hash-seed based) to prevent client code from relying on unstable iteration orders, though elements are stored compactly.

List.of(), Map.of(), and Set.of() accept a variable number of arguments up to 10 elements with specialized overloaded signatures to avoid varargs array allocation overhead; beyond 10 elements, Map.ofEntries() and general varargs overloads must be used.
Attempting to invoke any mutative operation such as add(), remove(), set(), or clear() on these collections throws an immediate UnsupportedOperationException at runtime.

parsed_answer.content: A classic production trap occurs when developers assume that List.of() makes the contained elements immutable as well. List.of() only freezes the collection structure; if you store mutable domain objects inside it (e.g., List.of(new User())), the internal state of those objects can still be mutated freely. To achieve true immutability, the objects referenced by the collection must also be immutable data classes (like Java records).
